# How to Prepare the Right Questions to Ask Your Doctor at Your Next Visit

> **In short:** You can turn a rushed, confusing doctor's appointment into a productive conversation by spending 10 minutes beforehand writing down your symptoms, your medical history, and your top three questions. This guide walks you through each step so you leave with real answers.

## Before you start

- **No special tools needed** — just a notepad or your phone's notes app
- **Time needed:** about 10–15 minutes the night before or morning of your visit
- **Who this is for:** anyone with an upcoming appointment who wants to feel more prepared and less anxious

## Step 1 — Track your symptoms for a few days before the visit

Write down what you have been feeling, when it started, and how it has changed. Include details like where the symptom is (lower back, top of head), what it feels like (aching, sharp, tingling), and whether anything makes it better or worse. Note how it affects your daily life — do you sleep less, avoid certain activities, or need more breaks at work? Even small symptoms matter because patterns help your doctor understand the bigger picture.

💬 Example: "For the past two weeks, I've had a dull headache on the right side of my head. It comes on around 2pm and gets worse if I've been on my computer all day. Taking a short walk outside usually helps."

You'll know it worked when you have a short written list that describes your symptoms clearly enough that someone else could understand them without you there to explain.

## Step 2 — Write down your medical history in one place

Before your appointment, gather the basics your doctor needs to know. This includes any past illnesses or surgeries, all medications you currently take (including vitamins, supplements, and over-the-counter pills), and any allergies. If you have seen other doctors recently, note what they said or did. You do not need a perfect memory — a simple list is enough.

💬 Example: "Current medications: lisinopril 10mg for blood pressure, vitamin D supplement. Allergies: penicillin causes a rash. Previous: knee surgery in 2019, diagnosed with mild asthma as a child."

You'll know it worked when you can hand your doctor (or show on your phone) a single list covering past conditions, current medications, and allergies.

## Step 3 — List your top three questions, starting with the most important

Think about what you really want to understand from this visit. Write down your questions in order of importance, putting the one that worries you most at the top. If you have more than three, write them all but flag your top three so you ask those first. Appointments often run short, so starting with what matters most means you will get answers to your biggest concerns even if time runs out.

💬 Example: "1. What is causing my headaches, and should I be worried? 2. Could my blood pressure medication be making them worse? 3. Are there any tests you would recommend?"

You'll know it worked when your three most important questions are clearly written and you plan to ask them first, before other topics come up.

## Step 4 — Bring a support person or use your phone to take notes

Ask a family member or close friend to come with you if you feel nervous or tend to forget details in the moment. Their presence can help you stay calm and they may think of questions you forgot. If you prefer to go alone, open the voice recorder on your phone before the appointment starts — most doctors are comfortable with this. Alternatively, take brief written notes during the visit so you can review them afterward.

💬 Example: "Before the doctor comes in, say out loud: 'I have a few questions written down — is it okay if I take notes during our talk?'"

You'll know it worked when you have written or recorded notes from the visit that you can review later, instead of relying only on memory.

## Step 5 — Ask for the next steps before you leave the room

Before the appointment ends, make sure you understand what happens next. Ask your doctor to clearly state the plan — whether that means starting a new medication, getting a blood test or scan, or changing something in your daily habits. Ask for written instructions if they are available. Also ask when you should follow up — next week, next month, or only if something changes.

💬 Example: "So to make sure I understand — you'll order an MRI, and I should hear from your office within a week about scheduling. Is that right? And if I don't hear by Friday, should I call you?"

You'll know it worked when you can repeat the next steps back to the doctor in your own words and they confirm you have it right.

## Common mistakes

- **Listing only vague symptoms:** Saying "I've been feeling off" does not give your doctor much to work with. Instead, describe the specific feeling, where it is, and when it happens.
- **Forgetting to mention supplements and vitamins:** Many people mention prescription medications but skip over-the-counter pills and supplements, which can interact with new prescriptions. Write everything down.
- **Leaving without asking about warning signs:** Always ask what symptoms should bring you back sooner than the scheduled follow-up. Knowing when to act fast reduces anxiety and prevents delayed care.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** You will feel more confident and less overwhelmed at appointments, especially when discussing sensitive or worrying symptoms.
- **For your family:** When you share your notes with other caregivers or specialists, everyone involved in your health has the same clear information.
- **If you are just getting started:** Spend five minutes right now writing down the one symptom that made you book this appointment. That single note is the most important thing you can bring.

## Try it now

Open your phone's notes app and write three sentences: what you have been feeling, when it started, and one question you want to ask your doctor. That is all you need to start.
